To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
infants 6 12 months of age spent most of their time in person engagement, while coordinated joint engagements increased in prevalence with age.
infants' attentional capabilities develop rapidly in the first 2 years of life and that they can coordinate attention with people and objects at an early age.

infants coordinate their attention to objects with their mothers and peers by 6 months of age, that they do so more often with their mothers, and that they become more skilled at coordinating their attention with their mothers and their peers as they develop.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of joint attention in infancy.
how infants learn to coordinate their attention to people, objects, and the world of experience.
the development of attentional coordination in social interaction and with the role of social partners in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the development of attention to objects and to social interaction proceeds in parallel, and that the two are coordinated by the end of the first year of life. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2005 APA, all rights reserved)
the development of attentional coordination with objects in early social interaction is not dependent on the partner's social competence.
infants coordinate their attention with others in the first two years of life, and that they do so more often with mothers than with peers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the development of joint attention is not simply a function of the infant's maturing cognitive and social skills. Rather
infants' attentional capabilities develop rapidly and in parallel across different partners.
mothers and infants are more similar than different.
The main takeaway from our work is that
infants' attention to objects is not independent of their attention to people, and that the coordination of attention to people and to objects is not a simple function of age or experience.
infants are not only capable of engaging in coordinated joint engagement with their mothers but also with their peers.
the developmental trajectory of joint engagement is similar regardless of partner and that the absolute amount of joint engagement is greater when the partner is a mother.
